paragraphs: Batch active learning chooses several examples to have labeled at each round. The challenge is to select a useful collection, rather than evaluate every candidate in isolation. This paper proposes choosing batches through a mutual information criterion connecting labeled and unlabeled examples. The criterion gives the selection process a statistical objective for deciding which queries to request together.

Within a Gaussian process framework, the authors express this selection task as a matrix partition problem. That formulation exposes a computational obstacle: finding the best partition is an NP-hard combinatorial problem. They therefore relax the discrete choices into a continuous optimization problem and apply a local optimization technique. The stated outcome is a good local solution, without a guarantee of finding the globally best batch.

The selection procedure is independent of the classification model ultimately used. This makes its information-based query strategy separable from the classifier itself. In the reported empirical studies, it performs comparably to or better than discriminative batch active learning methods, supporting its usefulness as an alternative approach to batch selection.
neurips-2010-active-instance-sampling-vi.tldr: An information-based batch selection method turns active learning into a relaxed matrix partition problem and obtains competitive empirical performance.

paragraphs: Many learning problems can be expressed as eigenproblems, connecting them to established numerical methods. Ordinary linear eigenvectors also have an optimization interpretation: they correspond to critical points of quadratic objectives under quadratic constraints. This paper extends that perspective to a particular class of problems whose objectives and constraints are nonquadratic.

The authors show how these problems can be understood as nonlinear eigenproblems and develop a corresponding generalization of the inverse power method. Their algorithm is guaranteed to converge to a nonlinear eigenvector. This guarantee concerns reaching an eigenvector within the proposed framework; it does not assert that every resulting solution is a global optimum of the associated optimization problem.

They apply the method to 1-spectral clustering and sparse principal component analysis, both of which fit naturally into the nonlinear formulation. For these applications, they report state-of-the-art solution quality and runtime. The broader contribution is a reusable connection between nonquadratic optimization and eigenvector computation, with the authors proposing that the method can be adapted to additional problems.
neurips-2010-an-inverse-power-method-for.tldr: A generalized inverse power method converges to nonlinear eigenvectors and achieves strong reported results in 1-spectral clustering and sparse PCA.

paragraphs: A joint statistical model must describe both the behavior of individual variables and their relationships with one another. This paper introduces a copula process that separates those two concerns. It describes dependence among arbitrarily many random variables independently of their marginal distributions, allowing the relationship structure to be modeled separately from each variable's own distribution.

The authors demonstrate the idea with Gaussian Copula Process Volatility, a model for predicting the unobserved standard deviations of a sequence of variables. These latent standard deviations represent the changing scale of variability. Predictions use Bayesian inference, with a Laplace approximation as one approach and Markov chain Monte Carlo as an alternative.

The model can outperform GARCH on the simulated and financial data considered. The authors also emphasize its ability to accommodate missing observations, use covariates beyond time, and represent a rich range of covariance structures. Together, these properties show how separating dependence from marginal behavior can support a flexible volatility model, alongside the reported predictive benefits.
neurips-2010-copula-processes-59e102e0e4.tldr: Copula processes separate dependence from marginal distributions and enable a flexible Bayesian volatility model that can outperform GARCH.

paragraphs: Decentralized optimization asks a network of participants to minimize a shared objective using only local computation and communication. Here, the shared objective is a sum of local convex functions, which may be nonsmooth. Each participant contributes part of the problem, while the network limits how information about those parts can travel.

The paper develops distributed algorithms based on dual averaging of subgradients and analyzes their convergence rates. A central feature of the analysis is that it separates progress attributable to the optimization method from the effects of restricted communication. This makes it possible to describe how network size and topology influence the time needed to reach a solution.

The required number of iterations scales inversely with the network's spectral gap, a quantity characterizing its communication structure. In this analysis, a smaller gap therefore implies more iterations. The authors support the sharpness of this dependence with theoretical lower bounds and simulations across different networks. The result ties computational progress to a concrete mathematical property of the network.
neurips-2010-distributed-dual-averaging-.tldr: Distributed dual averaging admits sharp convergence bounds that separate optimization progress from communication effects and depend inversely on the network's spectral gap.

paragraphs: Divisive normalization is a nonlinear transform proposed for efficiently representing natural sensory signals. This paper investigates why it works by connecting the transform to a statistical model of those signals. The relevant goal is to reduce dependencies between components of the representation, so that their joint behavior contains less statistical redundancy.

The analysis uses a multivariate t distribution to capture important properties of natural sensory inputs. Under this model, divisive normalization approximates a transform that would remove statistical dependence completely. The authors also use multi-information, a measure of joint dependence, to quantify how much dependence divisive normalization reduces. This provides a mathematical prediction that can be compared with its behavior on natural signals.

The theoretical analysis and quantitative evaluations support divisive normalization as an effective efficient coding transform. However, the paper also identifies a meaningful qualification: with a small pooling size, normalization may increase statistical dependencies. Its benefit therefore depends on how it pools information, and the model helps explain both its effectiveness and this possible reversal.
neurips-2010-divisive-normalization-just.tldr: A multivariate t model explains divisive normalization's dependency reduction while revealing that small pooling sizes may instead increase dependence.

paragraphs: The paper studies how to detect multiple change points across a collection of one-dimensional signals observed together. Its setting has an important shared structure: each change point occurs frequently among the signals. The problem therefore contains evidence across several signals about where changes happen, rather than treating every signal as an unrelated detection task.

The authors present a fast algorithm using group LARS to address this setting. The shared nature of the changes is central to the task being solved. A change point need not be described as occurring in every signal; the abstract specifies that it is frequently shared. This distinction allows the problem to concern common changes without requiring identical behavior throughout the collection.

The theoretical contribution gives conditions for consistency as the number of signals increases. That is a conditional claim about the method's behavior when more signals become available, rather than an unconditional guarantee for any collection. Empirical evidence supports these consistency results, connecting the analysis to observed behavior and making shared change detection the paper's main contribution.
neurips-2010-fast-detection-of-multiple-.tldr: A fast group LARS method detects change points frequently shared across signals, with conditional consistency results supported by empirical evidence.

paragraphs: Human motion perception may combine noisy measurements with prior expectations about how motion behaves. This paper tests the form of those expectations through human motion estimation tasks. The authors restrict their candidate priors to three ingredients: a preference for slow motion, first-order smoothness, and second-order smoothness.

They compare two mathematical forms for these ingredients: L2 regularization, corresponding to Gaussian priors, and L1 regularization, corresponding to Laplace priors. In an initial session, they estimate the weights that best fit human performance for each form. The Laplace version fits better, and the authors note that it also better matches natural motion statistics. Large fitted weights for second-order smoothness suggest that this higher-order property matters substantially in the tested judgments.

The researchers then use the fitted L1 models to predict performance in a second session with different experimental setups. They report excellent agreement across five subjects and ten conditions. This predictive test strengthens the evidence for a Laplace motion prior within the investigated family, while retaining the study's restriction to those candidate forms and motion properties.
neurips-2010-functional-form-of-motion-p.tldr: Human motion judgments favor Laplace over Gaussian priors in the tested models, with substantial weight on second-order smoothness.

paragraphs: This paper asks how the frequency of sensory stimuli should shape an efficiently organized neural population. Its focus is the allocation of cells and spikes: which stimuli receive more representational resources, and how strongly cells respond. The prior distribution over stimuli enters as a description of the sensory conditions the population is expected to encounter.

The model treats each cell's spikes as an independent Poisson process controlled by a tuning curve. It assumes that tuning width varies inversely with cell density and uses this relationship to approximate Fisher information. The authors optimize a family of objectives averaged over the sensory prior, including lower bounds associated with mutual information and perceptual discriminability.

For every objective considered, the optimum has a closed-form expression in which cell density and gain follow power laws of the stimulus prior. The theory also predicts a power-law relationship with discriminability. Preliminary empirical evidence supports links among stimulus frequencies, neural response properties, and discrimination thresholds. These observations support the model provisionally, alongside its explicit response and tuning assumptions.
neurips-2010-implicit-encoding-of-prior-.tldr: Under a specified neural response model, optimal cell density and gain encode stimulus priors through power laws, with preliminary empirical support.

paragraphs: Heavy-tailed distributions appear in many practical problems, but graphical models containing them often resist closed-form inference. This paper introduces the linear characteristic model, a linear graphical model built from independent latent random variables. Its defining move is to represent the model in the characteristic function domain, providing a different mathematical setting for inference.

The authors develop exact and approximate inference using stable distributions. This family encompasses Cauchy, Lévy, and Gaussian distributions, giving the construction access to several forms of distributional behavior. The contribution is an inference treatment for this linear multivariate setting. The model's definition is broader still: it exists for arbitrary random variables, including discrete, continuous, and mixed variables, although that broader definability is distinct from the stated stable-distribution inference results.

A realistic computer networking problem demonstrates the construction's applicability. The authors also identify iterative decoding over linear channels with non-Gaussian noise as a potential use. The paper thus links a general representation for linear random-variable models with concrete inference methods and an application beyond a purely mathematical formulation.
neurips-2010-inference-with-multivariate.tldr: Linear characteristic models enable exact and approximate inference for a linear multivariate setting using stable distributions.

paragraphs: Layered scene models represent surfaces that can move, overlap, and hide one another. This structure is appealing for estimating optical flow, but earlier layered methods had not matched the adoption or accuracy of non-layered approaches. The paper develops a probabilistic model designed to address several shortcomings together.

Its graphical model explicitly represents occlusion and disocclusion, the depth ordering of layers, and the consistency of layer assignments over time. Within each layer, motion combines a parametric component with a smooth deviation modeled through a Markov random field and a robust spatial prior. This combination allows layers to contain roughness. An image-dependent hidden field prior also helps define the layers, drawing on models of static scene segmentation.

These components connect motion estimation with decisions about surface membership and visibility. The reported method achieves state-of-the-art performance on the Middlebury benchmark while also producing meaningful scene segmentations and detecting occluded regions. Its contribution therefore includes a structured account of the scene as well as the estimated image motion.
neurips-2010-layered-image-motion-with-e.tldr: A probabilistic layered motion model combines visibility, depth order, and temporal consistency to produce strong optical flow results and meaningful segmentations.

paragraphs: Learning an object's features becomes difficult when the same feature can look different across appearances. The Transformed Indian Buffet Process addresses this by allowing inferred features to undergo transformations. The authors use it to construct a nonparametric Bayesian model, making variation across instances part of the feature-learning problem itself.

The model accounts for a previous human learning experiment involving features whose identity persists across changes in location. But allowing transformations creates an ambiguity: two observed parts might be distinct features, or transformed versions of one feature. A learner must also determine which transformations a feature can undergo. These questions connect feature identity to the surrounding learning context.

The paper introduces two experiments examining how people resolve these ambiguities. The model shows context sensitivity similar to that of human learners when determining which aspects of features remain invariant. The findings support transformation-aware feature learning as an account of the studied behavior, with context helping determine what counts as the same underlying feature across appearances.
neurips-2010-learning-invariant-features.tldr: The Transformed Indian Buffet Process models changing feature appearances and reproduces context sensitivity seen in human feature learning.

paragraphs: This paper studies the identification of sparse dynamic linear systems: learning a system's response while favoring a representation with fewer active components. It proposes a Bayesian nonparametric approach that combines two requirements in the statistical model. One concerns the stability of the learned responses, and the other concerns sparsity.

The system's impulse responses are modeled as Gaussian processes. Their autocovariances use the Stable Spline kernel to encode bounded-input, bounded-output stability, meaning that bounded inputs should produce bounded outputs. The authors then place exponential hyperpriors on the kernel scale factors to obtain sparse solutions. Stability is therefore represented through the covariance structure, while sparsity is encouraged through the scales controlling those structures.

Numerical experiments on ARMAX model estimation show an advantage over a group LAR algorithm and parametric identification methods based on prediction error minimization. These results support the proposed combination in the tested identification setting. The methodological contribution is to bring stability constraints and sparse estimation into one Bayesian framework for learning dynamic responses.
neurips-2010-learning-sparse-dynamic-lin.tldr: Stable Spline kernels and exponential scale hyperpriors combine stability and sparsity in Bayesian system identification, with advantages in reported ARMAX experiments.

paragraphs: Category learning involves deciding how objects should be grouped, but the usefulness of a grouping also depends on context. This paper treats those as connected learning problems. Its model learns both the organization of objects into categories and the circumstances in which that category knowledge should be applied.

The proposed account is hierarchical and Bayesian. Its explanatory focus is therefore broader than assigning an object to a category: it also includes learning when a conceptual representation is relevant. This matters because the same account must describe category structure and its context-specific use. Learning the context is part of the representation-building process described by the model, rather than an unrelated decision considered afterward.

The authors fit the model to multiple datasets and present it as a parsimonious description of human learning. The stated contribution is a compact account of how people acquire conceptual representations tied to context. Its significance lies in joining the content of category knowledge with the conditions for applying it within a single modeling approach.
neurips-2010-learning-the-context-of-a-c.tldr: A hierarchical Bayesian model jointly learns object categories and the contexts in which that knowledge should apply.

paragraphs: Counting cells or people in images need not require identifying every object's precise location. This paper proposes supervised learning of an image density whose integral over a region gives the number of objects there. Training uses images marked with one dot per object, connecting simple annotations to a representation designed specifically for counting.

The authors formulate density learning through a regularized quadratic risk objective. They introduce a loss suited to this task that can be evaluated efficiently with a maximum subarray algorithm. The resulting learning problem is a convex quadratic program solved through cutting-plane optimization. This provides a computational route from dot annotations and visual features to regional count estimates.

The framework accepts domain-specific visual features, so its counting formulation can be used with different image representations. The authors report accurate counts and little additional processing time beyond feature extraction after training. Those properties make it a candidate for real-time applications or large visual datasets, while its central contribution is estimating counts through density rather than requiring an individual detection for every object.
neurips-2010-learning-to-count-objects-i.tldr: Learning an image density from dot annotations enables accurate regional object counts with little overhead beyond feature extraction.

paragraphs: This paper introduces a family of online learning algorithms that work with a distribution of weight vectors. Their central concern is how that distribution moves during learning. By constraining its velocity flow, the method places structure on the changes made to the collection of possible weights.

The authors specialize this idea to a Gaussian weight distribution, describing its controlled evolution as herding. Learning balances constraints on that movement against a loss function representing predictive error. They show that uniformly bounding the loss makes the resulting optimization analytically solvable. This connects a distribution-based learning rule to an explicit mathematical solution for the optimization it requires.

Comparisons on a variety of real-world datasets show state-of-the-art robust performance, particularly when training labels contain substantial noise. That finding is empirical: it describes the behavior observed in the reported comparisons. The paper's contribution combines a new way to control online weight updates, a tractable optimization formulation, and evidence that the resulting algorithms handle noisy labels effectively.
neurips-2010-learning-via-gaussian-herdi.tldr: Gaussian herding controls the evolution of weight distributions and yields analytically solvable online updates with strong reported robustness to label noise.

paragraphs: Planning under partial observability requires reasoning about an unknown current state as well as future actions. POMCP addresses both tasks through sampling. It combines a Monte Carlo update of the agent's belief about the state with Monte Carlo tree search starting from that belief, using simulation throughout the planning process.

The method requires only a black-box simulator of the decision problem, rather than explicitly specified probability distributions. Sampling addresses dimensionality in both belief updates and planning, enabling effective planning in much larger problems. The authors demonstrate this on an expanded Rocksample benchmark and on two introduced tasks: 10×10 Battleship and Partially Observable PacMan, with approximately 10^18 and 10^56 states.

POMCP achieves high reported performance without prior domain knowledge. When supplied with simple domain knowledge, it can achieve better results with less search. These demonstrations support the practical value of combining sampled beliefs and sampled planning in a general-purpose method, including for very large problems whose state representation is unfactored.
neurips-2010-monte-carlo-planning-in-lar.tldr: POMCP combines sampled belief updates and tree search to plan effectively in enormous partially observable problems using only a simulator.

paragraphs: Multiple kernel learning chooses how to combine kernel functions for a prediction task. This paper studies the multi-label setting under the assumption that all classes share the same kernel combination. The objective is to find a combination that benefits the classes collectively, making computational scaling with the number of classes especially important.

Existing methods considered by the authors have computational costs that grow linearly with class count. They propose a framework combining worst-case analysis with stochastic approximation to reduce that dependence. Their analysis gives complexity O(m^(1/3)√ln m), where m is the number of classes. The stated class-count dependence grows more slowly than a linear one, addressing the bottleneck motivating the work.

In visual object recognition experiments, the proposed algorithm reaches classification accuracy similar to state-of-the-art multi-label multiple kernel learning methods while being significantly more efficient. The reported benefit is therefore computational efficiency with comparable accuracy. It applies within the paper's shared-kernel-combination formulation, which links the optimization across the classes.
neurips-2010-multi-label-multiple-kernel.tldr: Stochastic approximation reduces the class-count dependence of shared multiple kernel learning while preserving comparable accuracy in reported recognition experiments.

paragraphs: Differentially private analysis makes data available indirectly through noisy measurements. This paper asks what can be learned by treating those measurements as observations generated by a known measurement process. Its focus shifts from making each released value useful on its own to extracting information through probabilistic inference over the releases.

The proposed perspective derives posterior distributions over datasets and their model parameters using both the observations and the process that produced them. Accounting for the measurement process matters because noise is part of the evidence-generating mechanism. A posterior can describe multiple plausible underlying explanations and the uncertainty associated with them, rather than reducing the analysis to a single measured value.

The authors find that this approach can improve accuracy, combine multiple observations, and quantify uncertainty. It can also yield posterior distributions for quantities that were never directly measured. The contribution is thus a connection between private measurement and subsequent statistical analysis, showing how inference can make the available noisy evidence more useful for a broader set of questions.
neurips-2010-probabilistic-inference-and.tldr: Probabilistic inference over private measurements can improve accuracy, combine observations, and quantify uncertainty about measured and unmeasured quantities.

paragraphs: Generalized linear models are used to describe neural spike trains, and their relationship to point processes provides tools for checking model fit. One such tool uses time rescaling. However, the connection depends on assumptions that can break down when neural firing rates are high or observations are divided into coarse time intervals.

The paper shows how to retain point-process goodness-of-fit methods by constructing equivalent surrogate point processes from time-series observations. This construction supplies a way to apply those checks to GLMs despite the problem caused by discretization. The contribution concerns how model adequacy is assessed, making the representation used for testing an explicit part of the procedure.

The authors also introduce two further tests based on thinning and complementing point processes. These expand the available checks for both point-process models and discretized models. Together, the surrogate construction and additional tests address a concrete mismatch between observation format and testing assumptions, providing more ways to evaluate whether a fitted spike-train model adequately describes its data.
neurips-2010-rescaling-thinning-or-compl.tldr: Surrogate point processes and new thinning and complementing tests extend goodness-of-fit checking to discretized neural models.

paragraphs: Principal component analysis can be strongly affected by outliers. This paper considers corruption of entire data points, a setting relevant when a whole experiment, gene, or participant's contribution is unreliable. Such corruption requires a different recovery goal from problems where only a few components of each point are damaged.

The authors introduce Outlier Pursuit, an efficient convex optimization algorithm using matrix decomposition and nuclear norm minimization. Under stated mild assumptions on the uncorrupted points, the method recovers the exact optimal low-dimensional subspace and identifies corrupted points. The abstract notes that these assumptions are satisfied, for example, by a standard generative assumption used in PCA.

The target is the correct column space of the uncorrupted matrix, rather than exact reconstruction of the matrix itself. This distinction aligns the method with the underlying purpose of dimensionality reduction: recovering the structure supported by reliable observations. Identifying points that fail to conform to that structure is an additional output, making the method relevant when detecting contaminated observations is itself valuable.
neurips-2010-robust-pca-via-outlier-purs.tldr: Outlier Pursuit uses convex optimization to recover the underlying PCA subspace and identify corrupted points under assumptions on the clean data.

paragraphs: Support vector machines can capture relationships across many brain-image measurements. With a linear kernel, their learned patterns can also help locate differences between groups. Standard fitting, however, does not account for where features lie in the brain. The resulting pattern can be spatially scattered, making its anatomical meaning difficult to interpret.

This paper introduces spatial regularization based on a Laplacian framework. The framework can incorporate different constraints and works with both cortical surfaces and three-dimensional brain images. Its purpose is to make spatial and anatomical relationships part of classifier fitting, so that the model's discriminating pattern is shaped by more than the measurements considered without spatial structure.

The authors apply the method to magnetic resonance images from 30 patients with Alzheimer's disease and 30 elderly controls, using gray matter concentration maps and cortical thickness measures. The results demonstrate natural spatial and anatomical regularization of the classifier. The stated contribution centers on incorporating meaningful structure into the learned pattern and supporting its anatomical interpretation.
neurips-2010-spatial-and-anatomical-regu.tldr: Laplacian regularization incorporates spatial and anatomical structure into SVMs for more coherent brain-image discrimination patterns.

paragraphs: The LASSO estimates coefficients from noisy linear observations while encouraging a sparse answer through an L1 penalty. This paper asks how its estimation risk behaves as problem dimensions grow. An explicit description of that risk provides a way to characterize the estimator's performance beyond simply computing a solution for one dataset.

For sequences of observation matrices with independent, identically distributed Gaussian entries, the authors prove that normalized LASSO risk converges and derive an explicit expression for its limit. The result is an asymptotic theorem under a particular random-matrix assumption. Its proof uses analysis of approximate message passing, an efficient algorithm inspired by ideas from graphical models.

The authors also run simulations using real matrices from gene expression data and hospital medical records. These observations suggest that the theoretical results can be relevant across practical applications. The practical evidence complements the theorem: it explores usefulness beyond the precise matrix setting for which convergence and the limiting risk formula are rigorously established.
neurips-2010-the-lasso-risk-asymptotic-r.tldr: The paper derives an explicit asymptotic LASSO risk formula for Gaussian random matrices and explores its practical relevance through real-data simulations.

paragraphs: Several tasks can analyze the same image and produce related answers, such as identifying objects, estimating depth, and categorizing the scene. This paper develops a way to use those relationships while retaining existing classifiers as black boxes. The aim is to improve the tasks jointly without redesigning each classifier's internal operation.

Feedback Enabled Cascaded Classification Models use two layers containing repeated instances of the original classifiers. Outputs from the first layer become inputs to the second. Training maximizes the joint likelihood of the tasks and includes feedback from later classifiers to earlier ones. That feedback communicates which error modes earlier classifiers should focus on, connecting their training to the needs of the downstream stage.

The authors report significant improvements in every evaluated subtask across two domains. Scene understanding includes depth, scene and event categorization, object detection, geometric labeling, and saliency; robotic grasping includes grasp point detection and object classification. These results support combining correlated predictions with training feedback as a way to improve a collection of existing task-specific systems.
neurips-2010-towards-holistic-scene-unde.tldr: A two-layer classifier cascade uses training feedback to exploit related tasks and improves every evaluated subtask in scene understanding and robotic grasping.

paragraphs: Different clustering algorithms can produce very different groupings of the same data, and there may be no obvious single correct answer. This makes algorithm selection consequential but difficult. The paper proposes helping users compare clustering approaches through abstract properties of their input-output behavior, giving the choice a more explicit conceptual basis.

The authors show how intuitive properties of clustering functions can organize popular algorithmic paradigms into a taxonomy. They extend the approach from deterministic methods to randomized ones and use the resulting properties to distinguish common implementations of k-means. This makes differences in algorithm behavior visible even when methods share the same broad name.

They also study relationships among the properties independently of particular algorithms. This analysis strengthens Kleinberg's impossibility result and supplies a simpler proof. The work is presented as an initial step toward informed clustering selection: it offers a language for comparing behavior and understanding constraints on desirable properties, rather than resolving every choice of clustering method for a dataset.
neurips-2010-towards-property-based-clas.tldr: Abstract behavioral properties provide a taxonomy of clustering methods, distinguish k-means implementations, and strengthen an existing impossibility result.

paragraphs: The locust's lobula giant movement detector responds to approaching objects, with activity associated with escape behavior. A prevailing model, the eta function, describes this response by multiplying angular velocity by an exponential function of angular size. It predicts that activity peaks before contact, but unresolved inconsistencies motivate a more explicitly biophysical account.

The paper introduces the psi model, which connects angular size and angular velocity to biophysical quantities. It implements the multiplication associated with the eta function through divisive inhibition and avoids problems with directly implementing an exponential function. It also explains how activity peaks could occur after the time of contact, accommodating a response pattern outside the eta model's stated peak prediction.

The authors report consistent predictions of LGMD response features and excellent fits to published experimental data. Goodness of fit is comparable to corresponding eta-function fits. The contribution is therefore a model that retains strong agreement with observations while offering a biophysical explanation for the computation and a broader account of when response peaks can occur.
neurips-2011-emergence-of-multiplication.tldr: A biophysical LGMD model implements multiplication through divisive inhibition, explains possible post-contact peaks, and fits published data comparably to the eta model.
